messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: C++11 dependencies?
parts:
Is there any reason not to introduce C++11 dependencies
into Stan at this point?

I don't care if we ever get RStan on CRAN.

I'm asking because Michael's working on some new
features using C++11, but we haven't discussed whether
we're going to allow C++11 in Stan itself.

- Bob

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] C++11 dependencies?
parts: The only limitation is using a subset of the C++11 language that is supported by the compiler we are instructing users to use under Windows. That's g++ 4.6.3 prerelease. Unless someone can figure out how to install something else.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: C++11 dependencies?
parts:
On Monday, March 3, 2014 11:35:12 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Is there any reason not to introduce C++11 dependencies
into Stan at this point?  

I don't care if we ever get RStan on CRAN.  

I'm asking because Michael's working on some new
features using C++11, but we haven't discussed whether
we're going to allow C++11 in Stan itself.

Well, the next version of R to be released in late April is going to be the first to allow C++11 in CRAN packages

http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-devel/R-exts.html#Using-C_002b11-code

and I guess Rcpp will probably do so ASAP, so we should care even if RStan doesn't ever go on CRAN (which I still think it should).

My guess is that llvm-g++-4.2 on Mac is the sticking point, but clang++ is a viable alternative. For Windows, mingw based on g++-4.6 doesn't implement that much of the C++11 standard and ignores the -std=c++11 flag I think, but it should compile some C++11 stuff that was considered a g++ extension at the time.

Ben

The only limitation is using a subset of the C++11 language that is supported by the compiler we are instructing users to use under Windows. That's g++ 4.6.3 prerelease. Unless someone can figure out how to install something else.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: C++11 dependencies?
parts:
On Monday, March 3, 2014 11:55:57 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I thought Rcpp compiled (or at least used to) under C++11?
I think it does for everything except llvm-g++-4.2 on Mac.
Does it even matter for the level at which they're interfacing?

As long as CRAN sticks with its plan to have an option to build the binary Mac package with clang++, then probably not for most packages that depend on it. I haven't checked as to whether there would be any problems linking with a C++11 version of Rcpp if RStan doesn't specify -std=c++11.

Thanks for the tips on Windows and Mac.  

We absolutely need to keep compatibility with all platforms (Windows,
Mac, Linux), and both RStan and PyStan.

If we could get to the point where we say llvm-g++-4.2 isn't supported for RStan anymore, then we could at least use auto and decltype, which would be a lot cleaner than all the boost::promote_args<> stuff. I'm not sure if the mingw that comes with Rtools supports much more C++11 than that.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: C++11 dependencies?
parts:
Thanks very much for all the clarifications.

I'm happy deprecating support of llvm-g++-4.2. I think Apple's
pretty much doing that anyway.

That'd be awesome if we could replace Boost's promote_args with auto.
I'd imagine we could do it for internal variables that are declared
and defined in one go, but the compiler would have to be very smart
to figure out function return types, wouldn't it? For instance, if
we do something like this:

return x > 0 : var(x) : 0;

how can it figure out the return is var?

- Bob

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: C++11 dependencies?
parts:
On Monday, March 3, 2014 4:52:58 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Thanks very much for all the clarifications.

I'm happy deprecating support of llvm-g++-4.2.  I think Apple's
pretty much doing that anyway.
At the moment, we need llvm-g++-4.2 but hopefully that will all be squared away with the next Rcpp release.

That'd be awesome if we could replace Boost's promote_args with auto.
I'd imagine we could do it for internal variables that are declared
and defined in one go, but the compiler would have to be very smart
to figure out function return types, wouldn't it?  For instance, if
we do something like this:

  return x > 0 : var(x) : 0;

how can it figure out the return is var?

The short answer is that the compiler figures it out in much the same way that it figures out what template instantiations to do. The long answer is "I don't know how".

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: C++11 dependencies?
parts:
My compiler can't seem to figure it out, much as I suspected
it wouldn't be able to:

struct foo {
double x_;
foo(double x) : x_(x) { }
};

auto bar(double y) {
return (y > 0) ? foo(y) : 0.0;
}

int main() {
bar(12);
}

~/temp2$ clang++ --std=c++11 auto.cpp
auto.cpp:6:1: error: 'auto' return without trailing return type
auto bar(double y) {
^
auto.cpp:7:10: error: no viable conversion from 'foo' to 'int'
return (y > 0) ? foo(y) : 0.0;
^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
2 errors generated.

And this is the form of some of what we have now in the distributions.
But it turns out there's more magic in the form of decltype, so this
will work if I do this:

struct foo {
double x_;
foo(double x) : x_(x) { }
};

auto bar(double y) -> decltype(foo(0.0)) {
return y > 0 ? foo(y) : 0.0;
}

int main() {
bar(12);
}

But it's not very general --- decltype() just extracts the
type of an expression and the crazy-ass "->" syntax is
just telling you to use that for the auto return. The use
case is supposed to be when the type of foo changes but you
don't want to change the definition of bar.

The root problem is that the compiler doesn't know what
to do with this:

y > 0 ? foo(y) : 0.0;

or with:

if (y > 0)
return foo(y):
return 0.0;

It can't infer the required type. If we used boost promote to make
it a foo, no problem --- then the implicit constructor of foo gets
applied for the return.

- Bob
